body.statement: If \(f\), \(\theta'\), and \(\kappa\) are constant on \(J\), then \(T_n(P)=n^{1/3}|J|\{f\theta'^2/(4\kappa)\}^{1/3}\); once this deterministic horizon lies in \([T_0,\infty)\), Theorems 1--3 reduce to a stationary canonical LR maximum on that interval. At one fixed dose, the marginal statistic reduces to the Banerjee--Wellner law \(D(0)\).
body.justification: The reduction checks both the spatial factor and the fixed-point normalization against known theory.
body.gap: The fixed-dose reduction is known from Banerjee and Wellner (2001); the growing deterministic interval is the new simultaneous component.
body.consumer: It supplies an oracle simulation benchmark and a falsification check for implementations before applying heterogeneous clock estimation.

obligation.what_is_open: The homogeneous clock and fixed-location identities are proved, but the proposition's reference to the three unresolved growing-domain inference theorems cannot yet be certified.
obligation.obstruction: Substitution of constant coefficients determines the canonical interval length and fixed-origin functional but does not prove the canonical excursion, causal transfer, or feasible calibration laws.
obligation.attempted: The spatial integral was evaluated exactly, the canonical coordinate was shown affine, and translation of a single constraint location to the origin was checked.
obligation.partial_result:
If \(f(a)=f_0\), \(\theta'(a)=r_0\), and \(\kappa(a)=\kappa_0\) on \(J\), direct substitution into \(\texttt{def:spatial-clock}\) yields
\[
 \mathcal V(P)=|J|\left(\frac{f_0r_0^2}{4\kappa_0}\right)^{1/3},
 \qquad
 T_n(P)=n^{1/3}|J|\left(\frac{f_0r_0^2}{4\kappa_0}\right)^{1/3}.
\]
The canonical coordinate is affine in dose and maps \(J\) to an interval of exactly this length.  At one fixed dose, translation places the constraint at the origin, and the local functional is \(D(0)\) by \(\texttt{def:canonical-field}\).  These are the complete algebraic reductions.  They do not prove the canonical excursion, causal transfer, or feasible calibration assertions to which the current proposition refers.
